what_it_does: Solid-state drives (SSDs) store data in flash memory cells, and those cells gradually lose their charge when data is read many times — a problem called read disturb. The standard remedy is a read refresh: periodically re-writing threatened data to a fresh location before errors accumulate. Modern SSDs increasingly use a Zoned Namespace (ZNS) interface that organizes the drive into large, append-only zones (think of them as one-way filing cabinets that must be fully erased before reuse). The problem is that today's ZNS drives have no built-in mechanism to refresh individual blocks inside a zone; when a refresh is forced, it must move the entire zone's valid data — a huge, slow operation that chokes normal read/write traffic. FineRR-ZNS proposes letting the host software (the operating system or storage layer) track which blocks within a zone need refreshing and remap them to a small metadata log, so only the at-risk blocks are rewritten rather than the entire zone. A reconstruction method is also provided so the remapped data can be correctly reassembled when the application requests it.
